newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori says crisis will not knock Peru off track.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori says crisis will not knock Peru off track.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori insisted on Monday his government's deadlock with Marxist hostage-takers would not jeopardise Peru's delicate economic reform process.
"The isolated event of the takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence and the kidnapping of 73 people are not going to change our national direction," he said.

"This is fundamentally because, independent of the Peruvian government's firm political will, there exists the widest possible consensus among the population with regard to the need for peace and stability."
In six years of power, Fujimori had virtually defeated leftist guerrillas waging armed conflict since 1980 and transformed the Peruvian economy along free-market lines.

But the spectacular Dec. 17 takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels claiming to represent the poor revived memories of Peru's recent, bloody past and threatened to set back Fujimori's achievements.
In speeches to welcome two new ambassadors, Fujimori said the crisis would cause a minimum of damage to the nation.

"Peru has converted itself into one of the region's most attractive emerging markets," he said. "Peru continues on the path of progress. Investments in our country are totally guaranteed and the flow of investments has not stopped, proof that confidence in the country remains."

He said Peruvians were also united behind his tough stand against the MRTA. "The Peruvian people do not want to go backwards nor accept a return of violence and disorder to the country ... the peace and stability achieved are the pillars of our development."

The government and MRTA rebels holding the diplomatic residence remained deadlocked on Monday as the 73 VIP hostages spent their 34th day under the gun. Both sides say they are ready to talk but a face-to-face meeting is on hold because the goverment rules out considering the MRTA's main demand: the release of jailed comrades.
Reinforcing Peru's unflinching stand against the MRTA, Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto vowed on Monday never to give in to "terrorism."

"Terrorist activity is a grave challenge to all states and societies and it is vital for the international community to tackle terrorism in unity," Hashimoto said in a speech to Japan's parliament in Tokyo. He reiterated his "complete confidence" in Fujimori's refusal to discuss the release of 400 jailed MRTA members.

Underlining the stalemate in the crisis, there was little activity at the residence on Monday morning. One rebel briefly showed his face at a window of the residence and hostages were seen at windows hanging clothes out to dry.

The rebels have started to use the captives as workhands. One of the hostages spent nearly an hour on Sunday removing batteries from cars parked outside the building, which the rebels apparently plan to use in radios.
Peruvian daily Expreso reported on Monday that MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini was communicating with fellow rebels throughout Peru via coded radio messages.

"The messages that are being sent from the radio, according to the police, are camouflaged through a system of binary numbers whose content is only know by Cerpa and the comrades backing him up from outside the residence," Expreso said, adding that the code system was changed every week.
The remaining hostages inside the residence include Japanese businessmen and diplomats, Peruvian government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and Fujimori's younger brother Pedro.
